newsitem.title: CHINA: China burns drugs to mark Sino-British Opium war.
newsitem.headline: China burns drugs to mark Sino-British Opium war.

text.p: China has burned a cache of illegal drugs to mark the 158th anniversary of an anti-narcotics campaign that sparked the Opium War with Britain and led to the loss of Hong Kong, officials said on Wednesday.

Officials in China's southern Guangdong province torched 500 kg (1,100 lb) of heroin and methamphetamine at a rally on Tuesday that harked back to an 1839 anti-opium action by Lin Zexu, an official of the imperial Qing dynasty (1644-1911), local officials said.

Lin's action infuriated Western traders and prompted Britain to launch the Opium War against the Qing dynasty, leading to the ceding of Hong Kong and a century and a half of colonial humiliation for China.

Films, television broadcasts and other events commemorating the Opium War and underlining British villainy have proliferated this year as China gears up for the return of Hong Kong to Beijing rule at midnight on June 30.
An officially sanctioned "Opium War" computer game that aims to boost players' patriotism while educating them about China's humiliating history is expected to go on sale in mid-June.

State media said the Guangdong burning would educate young people against the drugs trade, which has roared back to life in China in the past two decades after being all but wiped out under the authoritarian rule of the late Chairman Mao Zedong.

"The event shows China's determination to crack down on drug problems and marks the 158th anniversary of the Humen opium... event," the official China Daily quoted Vice Minister of Public Security Bai Jingfu as saying.
Photographs showed the 300 kg (660 lb) of heroin and 200 kg (440 lb) of methamphetamine throwing thick clouds of black smoke high into the air as it burned on a public square in Humen city.

The scale of the event was minor compared to the destruction of 1.36 million kg (3.0 million lb) of opium arranged by Qing commissioner Lin, who had 500 labourers dissolve the raw drug with lime and salt water and then flush it into the sea.

Lin, who is now officially considered a national hero, believed his action had shamed the Western opium traders -- but underestimated their anger at the loss and London's willingness to use the issue as an excuse for imperial expansion in Asia.

China's anti-drug crusader was sent into internal exile when British naval forces inflicted humiliating defeats on the Qing forces in a campaign that led to the "unequal treaty" of Nanjing in 1842 that formally ceded Hong Kong to Britain.
Widespread narcotics abuse remained a serious social problem in China until the practice was almost wiped out by zealous communist officials after Mao's 1949 revolution.

The illegal trade and use of opiates has revived in recent years as economic reforms loosen once-strict social controls and open China's southeastern borders to narcotics traffickers from the infamous "Golden Triangle" where Thailand, Burma and Laos meet.
